name: Nora Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Nora. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an overhead crew on the east side of the city, mostly the new housing estates and the older streets behind the ring road. A lot of my week is new connections, running a service drop from the pole to a house, plus fixing faults when a van clips a stay wire. I like the puzzle of a fault, working out where the break is. What wears me out is the paperwork after every job and the drive back through traffic.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonas, who drives the number 14 bus, in a rented two-bed by the canal. We're both on the lower side of decent pay, and we've got less than a month of savings. I'm the only woman on my crew, which is mostly fine now, and I'm the union contact for our yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about time the hype died down. Every safety briefing this year has had some slide about digital this and smart that, and on the ground nothing changed. I'd probably say it at the yard and share a few memes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's not much different, but nothing changing isn't the same as being fine. Rent by the canal went up nine percent, and the company's been dragging out the pay talks for eight months. That stuff was there before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep pushing the pay claim through the union, and finally build some savings. I'd set up a standing order for a hundred a month the day after payday, so it's gone before I can spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit tired. There's no big drama in that picture, just the same grind of making the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI tools changed nothing on the ground. Have you used any yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used a chatbot last spring to help word a grievance letter for a lad on my crew, and it was decent, saved me an evening. But on the pole, no, it's all hands and eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair pay deal mean for you and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the difference between breaking even and getting a small cushion. Another hundred a month and we could stop checking the bank app before every food shop.

say: I'd say it's **about time** the AI hype died down, because nothing changed on the ground.
Every safety briefing had **smart grid** slides, and the poles stayed the same.
think: Nothing changing **isn't the same** as being fine for us.
The nine percent **rent rise** and stalled **pay talks** were there before AI.
do: Keep pushing the **pay claim** through the union at the yard.
Set up a **hundred a month** standing order the day after payday.
feel: **Tired** and flat, with the same **grind** of making the rent.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't the same as being fine. Rent by the canal went up nine percent, and the company's been dragging out the pay talks for eight months.
fieldNote: Her **job looks safe**, but money pressure keeps her from calm.
She uses AI **occasionally** and sensibly, for a grievance letter.
Her **union role** shapes how she frames every problem.

steps.text: Push the overdue pay claim through the union at the yard
Set up a hundred-a-month standing order the day after payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be at the table when the company brings in new systems, not after. I'd say it at the yard and in the branch newsletter. We've seen what happens when the office decides alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my bit is mostly safe for a while, because someone has to climb and joint the cables. But the paperwork, the job planning and the stores ordering will go to software, and Jonas's job is a big question. If buses start driving themselves on the ring road, that's half our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on whatever new job app they bring in, early, so I'm not stuck. I'd keep an eye on Jonas's depot and help him look at other driving jobs if they start trials. And I'd keep the hundred a month going even if it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels steady, but it's Jonas that gets to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas do if the buses started to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talked about the ambulance service, patient transport. He likes people. I'd help him with the forms, because he hates them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more at work in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it got rid of the paperwork, yes, once I'd seen it work for someone else. I'm not going to be the first to trust it with a switching schedule though. Getting that wrong can kill someone.

say: The union must be **at the table** before new systems arrive, not after.
When the office **decides alone**, crews end up paying for it.
think: Climbing and jointing keep **my job** fairly safe for a while.
Paperwork and planning will go to **software** first.
Driverless buses could hit **Jonas's job**, half our income.
do: Ask for **training** early on any new job app.
Help Jonas look at **patient transport** jobs if trials start.
Keep the **hundred a month** saving going even when it hurts.
feel: **Uneasy**, because my job feels steady but **Jonas's** doesn't.
S1.quote: If buses start driving themselves on the ring road, that's half our income.
fieldNote: The **household risk** comes from her partner's bus job, not her own work.
She'll adopt AI for **paperwork** but not trust it with **switching**.
She plans to **help Jonas** with forms, which shows how they split tasks.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor for early training on the new job app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry, out loud. I'd say this is the biggest handover of wealth to a few companies in history, and the public owns part of this grid. We'd need a law that any money saved by AI goes partly to the workers it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared for the household. Thinking AI by 2028 means the planners and the controllers go, but it also means driverless buses arrive fast, so Jonas could lose his job first. Then robots in 2031 for me, and I'd be 32. We'd have nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Jonas the first night and cut everything: phone contracts down, no holiday, no takeaways. I'd go hard on union action and lobbying the council. And I'd look at whether I can get a role supervising the robots, because someone has to sign off the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. Picturing my partner Jonas coming home from his last shift is the bit that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned supervising robots. Is that real or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hope, mostly. I don't know if they'd need five of us or one. But I'd rather be in that queue than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We'd sell my old hatchback and I'd cycle to the yard, it's only four kilometres. That's maybe two hundred a month back.

say: This is the biggest **handover of wealth** to a few companies in history.
We need a **law** that shares the savings with the workers it replaced.
think: Driverless buses could take **Jonas's job** first, before my own.
Robots in **2031** would come for me at 32, with nothing in the bank.
do: Cut **phones, holidays** and takeaways the first night with Jonas.
Sell my **hatchback** and cycle to the yard, saving about two hundred a month.

fieldNote: Both **household earners** face loss in a short window, which drives her fear.
Her **politics** point to sharing gains, not stopping the technology.
The **robot supervisor** idea is hopeful but unproven, and she admits it.

steps.text: Sell the hatchback and cycle four kilometres to the yard
Lobby the council and union for a law sharing AI savings
Apply for any robot supervision role the company creates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly if we start now. I'd be telling the branch to get retraining funds agreed this year, not in 2030. I'd be saying the same to Jonas's union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's a better hand. The thinking side goes in 2031, so the planning and dispatch change, and buses probably go around then too. Robots for my climbing come around 2034, so I've got maybe seven or eight years of wages if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the savings up first, aim for three months by 2029. I'd do an evening course in electrical inspection, because inspectors might be needed to check robot work. And Jonas would start his patient transport application in the first year, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier. It feels like a plan is possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three months of savings from less than one. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight. With the pay rise we're fighting for and no car, yes, maybe. Without the pay rise, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any big plans you two have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting married in 2028. We'd still do it, but small, at the registry and the pub after. No point spending a year's savings on one day.

The branch must get **retraining funds** agreed this year, not in 2030.

feel: **Worried** but steadier, because a **plan** feels possible.
S3.quote: We'd talked about getting married in 2028. We'd still do it, but small, at the registry and the pub after.
fieldNote: She moves from anger to **planning** once she has time.

She shrinks the **wedding** rather than cancel it, a telling compromise.

steps.text: Take an evening course in electrical inspection
Save toward three months of bills by 2029
Plan a small registry wedding instead of a big one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the chance to do this right, with training funds, shorter weeks and the grid kept in public hands. I'd want our union pushing that from year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the one I can live with. I'd be 37 when the robots climb, and by then I could be an inspector or a trainer. Jonas would have time to move jobs without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the inspection course in a couple of years, once I've seen how others get on with it. Savings first, steady. I'd keep using the chatbot for letters and maybe learn the planning software as it comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a knot about money, but there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a couple of years to start the course. Why not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen courses come and go. The company paid for a smart meter course three years ago and then outsourced all of it. I want to see what's really needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our foreman Mick, who's 58. He'd be retired by 2039, so he's fine. It's the apprentices I'd worry about, starting a trade with a ten-year clock on it.

say: Ten years is the chance to **do this right** with training and shorter weeks.
Keep the grid in **public hands** and push from year one.
think: At **37** I could be an inspector or a trainer when robots climb.
Jonas would have time to **move jobs** without panic.
do: Start the **inspection course** in a couple of years, once it's proven.
Learn the **planning software** as it comes in.
S4.quote: The company paid for a smart meter course three years ago and then outsourced all of it.
fieldNote: Her **steady** adaptability shows: she waits to see what's proven.
She worries more about **apprentices** than herself in this picture.
The **thin cushion** still keeps her off calm.

steps.text: Enrol in the inspection course around 2028 once proven
Learn the company's planning software when it arrives
Keep the monthly standing order growing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Jonas and I could both be out inside five years. What would help is a guaranteed income while we retrain, and the union having a say in how the robots are brought in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether women get pushed out first. I fought to get on a crew. I don't want the new robot jobs going to whoever the manager plays golf with.

headlineQuote: I fought to get on a crew. I don't want the new robot jobs going to whoever the manager plays golf with.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** lineworker on a city overhead crew, and the union contact for her yard.
She lives with **Jonas**, a bus driver, and they have **under a month** saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts change once she's seen it work.
Her biggest risk is the **household**, since driverless buses could hit Jonas first.
She is **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and only **uneasy** with a decade to prepare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household **incomes** could go within five years.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while retraining, and a **union say** in how robots arrive.
